extracted.intended_audience: creative writers and fiction critics interested in craft, aesthetics, and the relationship between body and prose
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Yukio Mishima's Sun and Steel principles to evaluate or produce fiction that integrates bodily discipline with literary form — focusing on form, control, transformative language, and ephemerality. Emphasizes sentence-level execution, decisiveness, and culturally specific aesthetic values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind–body integration (embodied craft)
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer's body is not separate from the writer's craft; disciplined physical training produces disciplined sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mishima argues from his own bodybuilding and martial-arts practice that a writer who cultivates only the mind produces 'dead' writing. Train the body alongside the imagination so prose acquires 'weight.' Anti-pattern: intellectualizing craft while neglecting physical discipline, which yields inert or detached prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words as acid / Transformative use of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Words inevitably distort reality; their power is to transform what they touch rather than simply represent it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mishima's metaphor: words are like stomach acid that corrode the stomach — language cannot be transparent. A strong piece exploits language's capacity to alter perception, not merely mimic external reality. Anti-pattern: strict mimetic realism that treats words as neutral windows onto reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against mimetic realism (avoid mere representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject attempting to 'represent' reality transparently; representation is surrendering language's real power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mishima recounts being chastised for refusing to 'represent' reality; he frames this as a defect. Instead of faithful depiction, aim for language that reshapes or intensifies experience. Example anti-pattern: faithful scene-reporting that fails to transform reader perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form (finished, sharp, definite prose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty of prose should be 'sharp, definite, finished' — sentences and structure should have clear, finished form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of three central aesthetic qualities (form, control, ephemerality). Evaluate whether sentences and overall structure feel complete and exactly articulated. Anti-pattern: formless or sprawling prose lacking finish or edge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control (disciplined restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery over chaos; disciplined restraint in language and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control is aesthetic restraint: does the writer exercise measured discipline rather than indulgence? Related to cleanness and decisiveness. Anti-pattern: overwriting, unnecessary ornamentation, or failure to pare language to essentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ephemerality (beauty held in the moment)
rubrics_metrics.description: An aesthetic valuing of the fleeting—beauty preserved only in a moment of perfection, with an emphasis on mortality and transience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mishima links ephemerality to the ideal of dying at the peak of beauty. Evaluate whether the work conveys urgency, transience, and the sense of stakes tied to mortality (the 'weight' of mortal stakes). Anti-pattern: treating beauty as durable or sentimental rather than momentary and intense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanness of execution (sentence-level precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences should be executed with cleanness — precise, unambiguous, and efficient like a well-forged cut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare a sentence to a sword stroke: it can be wasted, blunted, or perfectly placed. Assess sentence-level precision and whether each sentence does exactly what is needed. Scoring note: favor sentences that have no wasted movement or excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisiveness (commitment to hard choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer must make hard choices and commit; prose should display decisiveness rather than hedging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisiveness is evidenced by bold structural and stylistic choices and by avoiding equivocation. Related to 'cleanness' and 'control.' Anti-pattern: tentative prose that refuses to commit to an aesthetic or moral stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness of form to function
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose shape must be exactly what the matter requires — a fit between style/form and subject/intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the sword/pen analogy: the cut must do exactly what is needed. Ask whether the chosen form amplifies the subject matter or obstructs it. Anti-pattern: mismatches where ornate form distracts from content or blunt form flattens nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic of restraint (does the work restrain or overflow?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether the work practices restraint — holding back to increase intensity — rather than overflowing into excess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely tied to control; restraint increases aesthetic impact when used deliberately. Evaluate whether withholding, omission, or compression serves the work. Anti-pattern: over-explanation, excess detail, or gratuitous emotional display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ephemeral weight / mortal stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond ephemerality as form, prose should carry the 'weight' of mortal stakes — seriousness and gravity akin to life-and-death intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mishima links aesthetic perfection to preservation by death; in literary terms, evaluate whether the writing conveys seriousness and existential gravity. Works that treat stakes as trivial fail this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sword-and-pen virtues (cleanness, decisiveness, fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the martial and literary arts require cleanness of execution, decisiveness, and fitness of form to function; a sentence should be like a precise sword stroke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the analogy as a checklist: is the execution clean? Is the move decisive? Does the form exactly suit the effect sought? This synthesizes several related criteria into an overall martial-literary ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to cross-cultural aesthetic categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that Japanese aesthetic categories (yūgen, mono no aware, iki, wabi-sabi) produce different evaluation rubrics than typical Western workshop emphases (showing, telling, character arc, plot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying Mishima's standards, consider cultural aesthetics and how they shift priorities (e.g., valuing transience or refined chic over psychological realism). Avoid uncritically imposing Western workshop criteria on works operating in other aesthetic traditions.
